payload.claim: The clause-name fallback only survives one hop: after a citation that itself inherited its names from `prev_clause_names` (because its own clause was empty), line 148 sets `prev_clause_names = clause_names`, i.e. to the *literal* empty clause, discarding the inherited value instead of carrying it forward. So in a sentence with three or more citations sharing one name and no intervening backticked identifier, e.g. "`_foo` is called from three places (`a.py:10`, `b.py:20`, `a.py:30`).", the first two citations correctly get names=["_foo"], but the third gets names=[] and `_construct_defect` then always passes it (line 217's `if not spans: return None`), silently skipping the construct check for that citation even if its line range has drifted outside `_foo`. This contradicts acceptance criterion 2 ('A clause that names none takes the names of the clause before it in the same sentence'), which the `criteria: pass` gate result renders as satisfied. The fixtures only exercise two-citation chains ('`mod/lib.py:39`, `:43`' and '`mod/lib.py:5`, `:21`'), so no test exposes the break at the third citation.
